name: Gum recession treatment

image.caption: Receding Gums or Gingival Recession, Causes, and Treatment

lead: Gum recession treatment covers procedures that cover exposed roots and rebuild the gumline, mainly gum grafts from the palate or a donor matrix, plus flap techniques and growth-factor products. The payoff is shorter-looking teeth, an even gumline and a more natural smile.

Tissue is moved, grafted or regenerated over the exposed root and secured while it heals over about two to four weeks. Recession is very common: one meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources estimates about 85 percent of people worldwide have it on at least one tooth. Many registered trials compare grafts with collagen membranes, platelet-rich fibrin, placental membrane and other techniques.

paras: A periodontist chooses a technique based on how much recession there is and the bone and gum support. Treating the cause, such as gum disease, tooth position or brushing habits, is done alongside covering the root. Healing takes about two to four weeks.

Expect soreness, sensitivity and swelling while it heals, plus donor-site discomfort when palate tissue is used. Outcomes vary by technique and bone support, and if the cause of recession is not treated it can return.

angle.text: People treat gum recession, mostly with grafts, to cover exposed roots and restore an even gumline so teeth look natural in length. The visible coverage is the result of the procedure, and techniques are widely studied with results that vary.

lead: Gum recession treatment is the group of procedures used to cover exposed tooth roots and rebuild the gum line, so that teeth look the right length again and the smile shows even, pink gum framing the teeth rather than long, notched or darkened root surfaces [1]. Recession is common: a meta-analysis cited on Wikipedia estimates that about 85 percent of the world population has it on at least one tooth, and a 2026 study puts the figure at roughly 81 percent [1][2].

Most root-coverage procedures are gum grafts performed by a periodontist, usually under local anaesthesia. Tissue is moved from next to the recession, taken from the palate, or supplied by a donor dermal matrix, and then secured over the root while it heals over about two to four weeks [1]. Newer approaches add growth factors, platelet-rich fibrin, collagen or placental membranes, or tissue adhesives, and many of them have been compared in randomized trials [3][4][5][6][7][8].

Treatment of the cause is a separate matter from covering the root. Periodontal disease is the most common cause, and other reported contributors include thin gum tissue, tobacco, tooth position, trauma and piercings [1].
infobox: Miller classification most widely used; alternatives exist [1]
Pedicle graft, free gingival graft, connective tissue graft, acellular dermal matrix, growth-factor techniques [1]
About 2 to 4 weeks, results assessed after a few months [1]
About 81 to 85 percent of people have recession on at least one tooth [1][2]

paras: Recession is gradual and usually goes unnoticed until signs appear. Wikipedia lists teeth that look longer, visible exposed roots, a notch felt at the gum line, colour change, wider-looking spaces between teeth, tooth sensitivity to hot, cold, sweet or sour stimuli, and cavities below the gum line [1]. It is common in adults over 40 but can begin in adolescence [1]. Treating gum inflammation can sometimes reveal recession that swollen gums had hidden [1].

Periodontal disease is the most common cause. Other reported causes include rough or forceful brushing and flossing, hereditary thin or fragile gum tissue, dipping tobacco, self-inflicted trauma, scurvy, acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, crowded or misplaced teeth with thin bone cover, and lip or tongue piercings that rub the gum [1]. One review judged the evidence linking brushing to recession inconclusive, while a later study associated horizontal brushing, medium-hardness brushes and once-daily brushing with recession [1].

The Miller classification is the most widely used system for describing recession, though Wikipedia notes that many cases do not fit it and that alternatives exist, including the Kumar and Masamatti system, a separate palatal system and a newer scheme based on papilla position [1]. A registered study from 1987 onward followed 101 patients to analyse root-coverage stability over time [9].
A periodontist selects the technique according to the shape of the recession and the surrounding bone levels [1].

A pedicle graft repositions adjacent gum tissue over the exposed root. A free graft takes tissue from the palate, either as a free gingival graft or a subepithelial connective tissue graft [1]. A registered trial has tested a de-epithelialized free gingival graft in 60 participants [7].

An acellular dermal matrix, made from processed donated human skin, can replace palatal tissue [1]. A split-mouth trial registered in 2023 compared a xenogenic collagen membrane with connective tissue graft for multiple recession defects, and a trial of placental membrane for root coverage has also been registered [3][5].

subs.h: Growth factors, platelet concentrates and cell injections
paras: Wikipedia describes platelet-derived growth factor infused into bone graft material, combined with a cellular matrix and covered by an allograft, as improving integration with healthy bone and soft tissue [1]. Trials have tested platelet-rich fibrin alongside a coronally advanced flap [4][6]. A Russian report described three weekly injections of autogenous oral mucosa fibroblasts, with increased gum thickness and reduced recession lasting at least nine months [10].
A registered trial of 40 participants compares cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive with suturing for securing treatment of recession [8].

Healing takes about two to four weeks, results are assessed after a few months, and the new tissue sometimes needs a minor reshaping procedure [1]. Wikipedia states that complete or near-complete coverage is possible where there is no periodontal bone loss, a statement flagged there as needing a citation [1].

Most published work on root coverage consists of randomized and split-mouth trials of one technique against another, often with small groups. Registered trials include a xenogenic collagen membrane versus connective tissue graft in 8 participants [3], a coronally advanced flap with or without platelet-rich fibrin in 19 [4], placental membrane for root coverage in 15 [5], platelet-rich fibrin versus subepithelial connective tissue graft versus flap alone in 60 [6], a de-epithelialized free gingival graft in 60 [7], cyanoacrylate versus suture in 40 [8] and a comparison of two surgical techniques in 15 [11]. A further registered study will examine how keratinized tissue width and attached gingiva affect root coverage [12]. Outcome figures are not posted in these registry entries.
A report of autogenous oral mucosa fibroblast injections described statistically significant gains in gum thickness and reductions in recession lasting at least nine months [10].

A 2026 cross-sectional analysis evaluated the reliability and educational value of YouTube videos about gingival recession and its management, noting that more people now look for oral health information on digital platforms [2].
